content: Cylindrospermopsins (CYNs) are alkaloids characterized by a tricyclic guanidino moiety and uracil structure. These compounds are cytotoxic and primarily affect the liver, kidneys, and erythrocytes. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established a recreational guideline value of 6 µg/L for CYNs. They are produced by cyanobacteria such as Raphidiopsis (formerly Cylindrospermopsis), Anabaena (some now classified as Dolichospermum), Aphanizomenon, Chrysosporum, Oscillatoria, and Umezakia. In some regions, dissolved CYN concentrations are often equal to or higher than cell-bound CYNs and can persist for weeks even after the producing organisms are no longer present. Anatoxin-a (ATXs) is an amine alkaloid that acts as a neurotoxin by causing preand post-synaptic depolarization. ATXs are produced by cyanobacteria such as Anabaena (some now classified as Dolichospermum), Aphanizomenon (some now classified as Cuspidothrix or Chrysosporum), Raphidiopsis (formerly Cylindrospermopsis), Oscillatoria, Planktothrix, Phormidium, Tychonema, and Lyngbya (some now classified as Microcoleus or Moorea). Numerous deaths of dogs, livestock, and waterfowl have been attributed to the ingestion of scum containing ATXs, as well as detached lumps of benthic cyanobacteria or submerged vegetation with attached cyanobacteria washed ashore. Saxitoxins (STXs), also known as paralytic shellfish poisons, are alkaloids with many analogues. They are neurotoxic, blocking sodium (Na+), calcium (Ca++), and potassium (K+) channels in neuronal and cardiac cells. The WHO recreational guideline value for STXs is 30 µg/L. These toxins are produced by cyanobacteria such as Anabaena (some now classified as Dolichospermum), Planktothrix, Aphanizomenon (some now classified as Cuspidothrix or Chrysosporum), Raphidiopsis (formerly Cylindrospermopsis), Lyngbya (some now classified as Microcoleus or Moorea), and Oxynema (formerly Phormidium). Animal deaths have been linked to STXs in planktonic freshwater cyanobacteria. These toxins are also known from paralytic shellfish poisoning and are produced by some freshwater cyanobacteria. Freshwater mussels and crustaceans can accumulate STXs. Anatoxin-a(S) is an organophosphate neurotoxin that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. There is no WHO recreational guideline value for this toxin. It is produced by cyanobacteria such as Anabaena (some now classified as Dolichospermum), but its occurrence is sparsely documented. Harmful algal blooms (HABs) caused by cyanobacteria can lead to various health risks. In some cases, more severe symptoms like abdominal pain, muscle weakness, and fever have been reported. Cyanobacterial blooms are influenced by environmental factors such as nutrient concentrations, water mixing, and light availability. High nutrient levels, particularly phosphorus, promote the dominance of cyanobacteria. In water bodies with low nutrient concentrations, cyanobacteria are less likely to form prolonged blooms. However, buoyant cyanobacteria can rise to the surface and form scums, which may accumulate along shorelines or in bays. These scums can pose health risks, especially if they contain high levels of toxins. Management of cyanobacterial blooms involves reducing nutrient loads, particularly phosphorus, from catchment areas. This process often requires years to decades to achieve significant reductions in cyanobacterial biomass. Surveillance strategies should prioritize sites with high public health relevance and include visual assessments, sampling, and toxin analyses when appropriate. Recreational water safety can be maintained by avoiding direct contact with cyanobacterial scums or floating mats. Informing site users about potential risks and providing clear guidance on safe water use are essential. Sustainable management of water bodies to prevent blooms includes reducing nutrient inputs and implementing long-term interventions to limit eutrophication.
